title: My friends left Ukraine after the Russian invasion. Now I wonder if we live in the same world | Diana Berg
summary:
Anger, guilt, shame: the deepest unseen wound of this war is the rift between those who left and those who stayed behind

“Can we reschedule?”

Over the years of working with western colleagues, I had learned to accept that they don’t fully understand what war feels like from the inside. They would ask me to find someone in occupied Mariupol for an interview, or seem genuinely puzzled that I couldn’t just log on at a time that suited them. I made my peace with this long ago – they don’t have to understand. But this time, it was a Ukrainian who asked.

Diana Berg is a Ukrainian artist, writer and cultural manager from Mariupol, and the founder of Platform TU, an independent cultural initiative now operating in exile after Russia’s full-scale invasion.

title: Andy Burnham’s plans could bring the UK closer to Europe than he realises
summary:
The new PM’s priorities are domestic, but he will soon realise that closer engagement with the EU is a no-brainer

What will European leaders make of Andy Burnham, the seventh UK prime minister they have had to deal with in a decade of chronic political instability in London unleashed by the fateful 2016 referendum vote to leave the European Union?

The “king of the north” is largely an unknown quantity in continental Europe and has given priority to a domestic agenda of devolving powers to regions and cities and extending state control of vital industries rather than to foreign policy. He may initially spend less time on diplomacy than his predecessor, Keir Starmer, whom critics branded “never here Keir” for his frequent foreign travel to support Ukraine, build European and Nato defence ties and try to rein in Donald Trump’s wrecking instincts in transatlantic relations.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Mykhailo Drapatyi takes over as Kyiv’s top commander
summary:
Zelenskyy hopes to end debacle over sacking of defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov; Kremlin’s sympathies for Wildberries. What we know on day 1,610

Medium and long-range strikes against Russia will continue under Mykhailo Drapatyi, Ukraine’s new top military commander, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday, as he replaced Oleksandr Syrskyi in the job after a huge political row accompanied by street protests. “The operations of the Ukrainian defence forces are ​ongoing and must continue steadily,” said the Ukrainian president. “Ukraine’s plan for long-range sanctions and our ‌programme of middle-range strikes will be carried ‌out with absolute precision.”

Luke Harding writes that news of Drapatyi’s appointment came in a late-night TV address by Zelenskyy. The president offered a “prominent position” to Mykhailo Fedorov – the defence minister he sacked last week in a shock move that brought out protesters who have given a deadline of Friday for Fedorov to be reinstated. Fedorov welcomed Drapatyi’s appointment as a “breath of fresh air” bringing “new hope to the struggle of free people for freedom and justice”.

Zelenskyy paid tribute to Syrskyi, crediting him with leading the defence of Kyiv and launching a counter-invasion of Russia’s Kursk province. Drapatyi, his replacement, is well regarded within Ukraine’s army and liked by the public, Harding writes. He is viewed as an ally of Fedorov, a tech-savvy moderniser. A major general, Drapatyi is commander of Ukraine’s joint forces group and has been fighting Russia since its covert attempt in 2014 to take over the eastern Donbas region. He is famed for driving an infantry fighting vehicle over a barricade set up by pro-Russian militants in Mariupol.

The Kremlin lamented the Ukrainian attacks on warehouses of Wildberries – an Amazon-like chain that Kyiv says supplies drone parts and other technologies for the Russian war effort. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov ​said: “The situation is indeed difficult because of the losses suffered ‌both by the company itself and ‌by representatives of small and medium-sized businesses.”

Russian authorities are taking fuel away from Siberia and giving it to Moscow – Russia’s wealthiest and most populous region, where Vladimir Putin most fears losing the support of the Russian elite. The success of Ukrainian drone attacks on oil refineries, storage and shipping has caused fuel crises of varying degrees across Russia. Traders told Reuters that to replace lost production, gasoline produced in the Urals and Siberia, as ⁠well as imported supplies from Belarus, has been redirected to the Moscow region. One of the traders ​said the Achinsk refinery in Siberia’s Krasnoyarsk ​region has been supplying Moscow with fuel.

Civilian injuries and deaths increased by more than a third in Ukraine ⁠in the first half of the year, the UN human rights office ⁠said. It documented 1,396 deaths and 7,978 injuries in ⁠the first six months of 2026, representing a 37% increase from the same period last year and a near ⁠doubling versus 2024. Long-range ballistic missiles and drones, and short-range drones and glide bombs drove the escalation.

A Russian guided-bomb attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia killed ⁠at least three ⁠people ​on Tuesday and injured more than a dozen, regional officials said. Two of the dead were ​in their 60s and the other ‌was 49. Seven floors of ⁠a nine-storey apartment block were engulfed by flames after the attack, the regional military administration said.
